passage: I'm Tanuja, and I live upstairs from Hrithik. Twice this monsoon the town had flood warnings, and twice the water stopped at the road. So on Monday, when the siren went again, I packed a bag and knocked on Hrithik's door. "Same as last time, it'll pass," Hrithik said, and turned the television up. By evening the drain outside was gurgling. At nine the water was over the doorstep, and by ten the lane to the main road had vanished under brown water and nobody could leave. Hrithik carried a suitcase up to my flat and stood on the stairs with a phone in hand, saying nothing. Downstairs the mattress and books were already soaked and the power was out. I felt sick watching the water climb. I don't know what was in Hrithik's mind. I only know the earlier warnings had been harmless.

qa.a: At nine the water was over the doorstep.

qa.a: Hrithik could have left with Tanuja when the siren first went, because a warning that ended harmlessly before does not mean the next will, and routes get cut once the water rises.

passage:
Monday. The warning said heavy rain and possible flooding in their Patna colony. Baljeet read it and shrugged. "Last year they said the same. The water stopped at the main road." His cousin Abhinav, visiting from Delhi, asked if they should move to his aunt's place on higher ground. "No need," Baljeet said.
Tuesday. It rained all day. By evening the street was ankle-deep. Neighbours were loading tempos. Baljeet stacked the rice sacks on the bed and stayed. "It'll drain overnight."
Wednesday, dawn. Abhinav woke him: water was coming under the door. By seven it was knee-deep on the ground floor. They tried to leave, but the lane to the main road had become a fast brown stream, and the tempos had gone.
They waited on the roof for four hours with Baljeet's grandfather until a rescue boat reached them. On the boat, Baljeet didn't speak. He had been so sure.

qa.a: They waited on the roof for four hours.

qa.q: What does Baljeet's silence on the boat suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt shocked and ashamed, realising his certainty had put the family in danger.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Baljeet responded to the warning?
qa.a: I would leave for the aunt's place on Monday when Abhinav suggested it, because past warnings passing safely didn't mean this one would.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have felt during those days?
qa.a: Abhinav probably felt uneasy and frustrated, suggesting they move early and then waking to water under the door.

passage:
"Saurabh, you ask why I leave the moment they announce a warning. I'll tell you, since I'm Joseph, and I once didn't.
I was twenty, living with my parents near the river in Kerala. Every monsoon there were warnings, and every monsoon the water came to our gate and stopped. So when the big alert came, I told Amma, 'Same as always.' Neighbours left. We didn't.
On the second night I heard water in the kitchen. By morning it was up to the windowsills. The road to the church on the hill was gone, completely under.
We climbed to the neighbour's terrace and waited a whole day. Fishermen from the coast came in their boats and took us out.
I kept thinking: every warning before had passed, so I thought this one would too. That's what nearly cost us."

qa.q: Who took Joseph's family out of the flood?
qa.a: Fishermen from the coast came in their boats and took them out.

qa.q: What was young Joseph thinking when the big alert came, and how did Joseph feel?
qa.a: Joseph felt confident and unworried, telling Amma it was the same as always because earlier warnings had passed.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Joseph's story, and what should have been different?
qa.a: Deciding to stay when neighbours left was the turning point; leaving when the alert came would have avoided the terrace and the rescue.

qa.q: How might Joseph's mother have felt on the terrace?
qa.a: Amma was likely frightened and exhausted, waiting a whole day for rescue after trusting that it would be the same as always.

grounding: Shows a person, used to warnings passing harmlessly, staying put until floodwater is inside and the road out is cut.
